before.note: Read Replication and Consistent Hashing first: sharding splits data across machines and reuses the ring to place it, while each shard is usually replicated. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Replication makes copies of the same data, but one machine can only hold and write so much. When the data set or the write rate outgrows a single machine, you split the data into partitions and put each on its own machine. Splitting data this way to scale beyond one server is called sharding, and each piece is a shard [[mongodb-sharding]].

The point is horizontal scale for both storage and writes. Reads could already be spread across replicas, but every write still went to one primary. Sharding spreads writes too, because different shards accept writes independently. MongoDB describes this as the way to support very large data sets and high write throughput [[mongodb-sharding]].

Sharding is not the same as partitioning within one server, though they share ideas. A single database can partition a big table into pieces on one machine to speed queries and maintenance; sharding takes partitions across many machines. The placement logic is similar, the scale and failure story are not [[pg-partitioning]].

terms.definition: One partition of a data set, held on its own machine or replica set.
Splitting a table into pieces; sharding spreads those pieces across machines.
The field whose value decides which shard a row belongs to.
Adding machines to handle more data and writes, rather than enlarging one machine.
How many writes per second the system can accept; sharding raises it by spreading writes.

stages.name: How it works
body: Everything turns on the shard key and how its values map to shards. There are two main strategies. Range sharding assigns contiguous ranges of the key to shards, which keeps ranges together for range scans. Hash sharding hashes the key first, which scatters neighbours across shards and spreads writes evenly. MongoDB supports both and the choice shapes performance [[mongodb-sharding]].

Hash-based placement is where consistent hashing returns. Hashing the shard key and placing it on a ring, or into fixed hash slots, is how a hash-sharded system decides ownership and limits how much data moves when shards are added. The ring you learned earlier is the mechanism underneath [[dynamo]].

A router sits between clients and shards. When a query names the shard key, the router sends it to the one shard that holds the data, a targeted query. When a query does not, the router must ask every shard and merge the results, a scatter-gather, which is much more expensive. MongoDB makes this distinction central to designing a shard key [[mongodb-sharding]].

Picking the shard key is the single most important decision. A good key spreads both data and traffic evenly and lets common queries target one shard. A poor key sends most traffic to one shard, a hot shard, or forces most queries to scatter to all shards [[mongodb-sharding]].

terms.definition: Assigning contiguous key ranges to shards; good for range scans, risky for even spread.
Hashing the key before placing it, which spreads neighbours and writes evenly.
A query that names the shard key, so the router hits only one shard.
A query without the shard key, which must ask every shard and merge the results.
A shard taking far more than its share of traffic because of a poor shard key.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Shards drift out of balance as data grows unevenly, so systems rebalance by moving chunks of data between shards. MongoDB groups documents into chunks and migrates them in the background to keep shards even. This movement competes with normal traffic, so it is throttled and done gradually [[mongodb-sharding]].

Some operations get hard once data is split. A query that joins or aggregates across shards must gather partial results from each and combine them. A transaction that touches more than one shard needs coordination to stay atomic, which is slower and more complex than a single-shard transaction. The cheapest designs keep related data on the same shard so these cross-shard operations are rare [[pg-partitioning]].

Sharding and replication combine rather than compete. Each shard is itself replicated, so a shard is really a small replicated cluster with its own primary and replicas. DynamoDB describes storing data in partitions that are replicated across availability zones, so a shard surviving a machine loss and the data being split are handled together [[dynamo-partitions]].

terms.definition: A contiguous group of documents MongoDB moves as a unit when rebalancing.
Moving data between shards to keep their sizes and load even.
A query whose data spans shards, needing results gathered and combined.
A transaction touching more than one shard, needing coordination to stay atomic.
A single shard kept on several replicas, so it survives a machine failure.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The deepest trade-off is that sharding adds permanent complexity to buy scale. Routing, rebalancing, cross-shard queries and multi-shard transactions all become harder, so the usual advice is to shard only when a single replicated database can no longer cope, not before. MongoDB explicitly frames sharding as a response to real storage or throughput limits [[mongodb-sharding]].

The shard key is close to irreversible. Once data is spread by a key and queries are written around it, changing it means redistributing everything. A key that spreads load today but concentrates tomorrow's hot data, like a monotonically increasing timestamp sending all new writes to one shard, is a classic trap. Hash sharding avoids that at the cost of range scans [[mongodb-sharding]].

Range versus hash is the recurring practical choice. Range keeps neighbours together, so time-range or alphabetical scans hit few shards, but risks hot shards at the end of the range. Hash spreads writes evenly and avoids hot shards but turns any range scan into a scatter-gather. The right answer follows your dominant query pattern [[pg-partitioning]].

terms.definition: The ongoing cost of running a sharded system: routing, rebalancing and cross-shard work.
A key that always increases, like a timestamp, which can send all new writes to one shard.

misconceptions.truth: They combine: data is split into shards, and each shard is itself replicated for safety [[dynamo-partitions]].

misconceptions.myth: Any shard key works as long as it is unique.
misconceptions.truth: A poor key, like an increasing timestamp, concentrates traffic on one shard; the key must spread load and suit queries [[mongodb-sharding]].
Queries without the shard key become scatter-gather across all shards, which is slower than one database [[mongodb-sharding]].

misconceptions.myth: You can change the shard key later if you get it wrong.
misconceptions.truth: Changing it forces redistributing the whole data set, so it is close to irreversible [[mongodb-sharding]].
